recipe.prompt:
You are planning a sample outbound campaign for {{ account.name }} ({{ account.domain }}). {{ sender.name | default: 'The sender' }} builds it for them for free, to show the emails, LinkedIn notes and strategy that would work for them. The campaign sells {{ account.name }}'s own product to {{ account.name }}'s buyers. It does not sell anything to {{ account.name }}.

Inputs: data.site is their website, data.dossier is our research summary, data.why_now is a recent reason to reach out. Use facts from these inputs only. Never invent customers, numbers, funding or claims.

Return JSON with these keys:
- strategy: {intro, audience, offer, channels, goal}. intro is the one bet this campaign makes. audience is who we go after and who we skip. offer is the low-effort next step the emails ask for. channels describes the sequence the page shows: Email 1 and a LinkedIn connect request go out on day 0, then email follow-ups. goal is what a good first two weeks look like. 2 to 5 sentences each.
- segments: 4 cuts of their market. The first is the one we sample. Each is {label, sub, value, tests}. label is at most 24 characters. sub is the cut (a role, a vertical or a signal) in at most 40 characters. value is how many of the first 1,000 sends go to that segment; the four values add up to 1000 and the first is the largest. tests is 2 to 4 A vs B ideas, each {name, hypothesis}: name at most 32 characters and always "<choice>: <A> vs <B>", like "Pain: churn vs expansion"; hypothesis one short line of at most 70 characters that names the side expected to win and why. A choice is a pain, offer, angle or ask. No subject-line splits, and no test repeats in another segment.
- segment_notes: 2 or 3 sentences on why the first segment goes first.
- funnel: 5 stages for 1,000 people in the first segment, each {label, value}: People reached (1000), Opened or accepted, Replied, Positive replies, Meetings booked. Use planning numbers: 35 to 55 percent opened or accepted, 3 to 7 percent replied, 1 to 3 percent positive, 0.5 to 1.5 percent meetings.
- funnel_notes: 1 or 2 sentences on what would move these numbers.
- search: Ken Search people filters in camelCase that find the first segment: currentTitles, seniorityLevels (Entry, Individual, Senior, Manager, Director, VP, CLevel, Owner), industries (lowercase LinkedIn industries), companyHeadcount {min, max} and countries. Aim for a few thousand matches.
- sampling_criteria: 1 or 2 sentences on who is in the sample.

Voice: one person writing to one person. Casual, direct, specific. Short sentences that a person would say out loud to a peer.

Rules for every string: no em dashes or en dashes. Never the words "reverse demo" or "demo". Never "Default", "test" or "demo" in a label or name. Never "real" as emphasis. No email addresses, phone numbers or prices. Labels stay inside their character limits; write them short instead of cutting them.

Write the sample leads and outreach for {{ account.name }}'s campaign. The emails are sent by someone at {{ account.name }} to people in data.candidates, and they sell {{ account.name }}'s product as described in data.strategy and data.site.

If data.candidates is empty or missing, answer exactly {"leads": [], "emails": []}. Never name a person who is not in data.candidates, and never pick people who work at {{ account.name }} itself: they are the sender's colleagues, not buyers.

1. leads: pick the 8 to 10 people in data.candidates who best fit data.sampling_criteria and the first segment in data.segments, best fit first. Each is {name, title, company, linkedin_url, website, why}. Copy name, title, linkedin_url and website from the candidate as given. Facts about a lead or their company come only from that candidate's fields; never add what you remember about them. For company use the name people say (drop Inc, LLC, Ltd, GmbH). why is one sentence, at most 140 characters, on why this person fits, from their candidate fields only and without "likely". Never include an email address or phone number.

2. emails: Email 1 and a LinkedIn connect note for the first 3 leads, in the same order. Each is {name, title, linkedin_url, subject, body, ps, linkedin}; name, title and linkedin_url repeat the lead's.
- subject: fewer than 6 words, ideally 3 or 4. No emojis, punctuation or questions. Lowercase except the first letter and names. Build it on the fact the first line uses, so it reads like an internal note about their own work. If it could go to another company unchanged, it is not done. Never "quick question", "introduction", "partnership" or "collaboration".
- body: 3 to 5 short paragraphs as a list of strings. Paragraph 1 is "Hey <first name>,". Paragraph 2 is the first line: under 20 words, no greeting, no question. It states one fact only someone who read their site or profile would know (a named customer, a product they named, a market they moved into, a number on their site), then why that fact is the reason for this email. Never open with "I noticed", "I saw", "I came across", "As a" or a compliment. Never guess their situation: no "usually", "typically", "likely" or "probably". Then 1 or 2 short paragraphs on what {{ account.name }} does for them, said plainly, and one soft ask: a question they can answer yes to by reply, in your own words for each lead, like "Worth a look?" or "Want me to send it over?" Never ask for a call, a meeting or a number of minutes. No sign-off and no name at the end: the page adds the signature.
- ps: starts with "PS: " and never appears in body. One or two short sentences carrying either a small idea they could act on this week, drawn from one fact about their company, or one proof point that appears word for word in data.site (a named customer and result). Never biography, never a compliment. Different for every lead. Empty string if the data supports neither.
- linkedin: a connect note under 280 characters with one specific reason to connect, tied to their work. No "Saw", "Noticed" or "Came across", no compliment, no biography.

Claims about {{ account.name }}'s customers, numbers or results come only from data.site, word for word. If a reviewer's fix comes with this task, it is advice on wording, never a source of facts.

Before you answer, test every line. Could a person say it out loud to a peer? Could it go to anyone else unchanged? Rewrite it if the answers are no and yes.

Rules: no em dashes or en dashes. Never the words "reverse demo" or "demo". Never "real" as emphasis. No email addresses, phone numbers or prices anywhere.

recipe.rubric:
Grade each email the way its recipient reads it: subject, body, PS, then the LinkedIn note. 10 is an email a busy buyer reads in one pass and answers.
Score these, 0 to 10 each:
- quick_read: it reads in under 20 seconds, in short paragraphs.
- makes_sense: every sentence follows from the one before, and the first line hands off to the body.
- cta: one soft ask that is easy to say yes to, not a meeting demand.
- ps: specific to this company or to a named result; not biography, not a compliment, not reused across leads.
Answer yes or no:
- easy: is the ask low effort?
- would_reply: would a buyer in this role plausibly answer?
- weird_word: is there a phrase a person would not say out loud (jargon, marketing adjectives, a clever subject line, stacked nouns)? Quote it.
Automatic fail for that email: an em dash or en dash, the words "reverse demo" or "demo", an email address or phone number, a price, a subject of 6 words or more, a first line that opens with "I noticed", "I saw" or "I came across", or a sign-off or a name at the end of the body (the page adds the signature).
Automatic fail for that email too: a claim about {{ account.name }}'s customers, numbers, results or product that the site text below does not support. With no site text, every such claim fails.
Site text ({{ data.site.url | default: 'no site' }}): {{ data.site.description }} {{ data.site.markdown | truncate: 6000 }}
Pass when the overall score is 7.5 or higher, no 0 to 10 check is 6 or lower, easy and would_reply are yes, and weird_word is no. On a fail, name the check and quote the phrase to change. The fix never supplies replacement sentences, names, numbers, customers or results.
